speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: asked the Prime Minister with regard to the stern warnings issued to six former staff of Keppel Offshore & Marine Limited (a) whether the reasons for issuing stern warnings in lieu of prosecution for offences punishable under the Prevention of Corruption Act 1960 can be elaborated upon; and (b) what is the assessed reputation damage to Singapore arising from the case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: asked the Prime Minister regarding CPIB's decision not to prosecute six former employees of Keppel Offshore & Marine Limited (KOM) due to evidentiary difficulties (a) whether the statement of facts which KOM agreed to as part of a plea agreement with the United States Department of Justice and the admissions made in the United States proceedings by KOM's former legal counsel who is based in Singapore were considered; and (b) if so, why were these considered as insufficient in overcoming the said difficulties.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Prime Minister why the statement of facts contained in the Deferred Prosecution Agreement concluded between Keppel Offshore & Marine Limited with the United States Department of Justice dated 22 December 2017 is not considered sufficient, available, and appropriate evidence of the six former senior management staff's culpability for them to be charged with corruption in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: asked the Prime Minister whether other agencies apart from the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau and Attorney-General's Chambers, have been consulted on the issue of the appropriate action to be taken on former staff of Keppel Offshore & Marine Limited who are involved in bribe payments and, if so, what are those views.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: asked the Prime Minister based on investigations into the Keppel Offshore & Marine Limited corruption case conducted by CPIB (a) what are the offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act 1960 (PCA) that were considered for prosecution for the six individuals; and (b) what is the maximum penalty for these offences under the PCA.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: asked the Prime Minister in deciding against prosecuting the six individuals involved in the Keppel Offshore & Marine Limited corruption case (a) what weightage has been given to the various relevant factors such as the culpability of each individual, the available evidence and what is appropriate in the circumstances; and (b) whether this is consistent with the Government’s political commitment and leadership and a culture of zero tolerance against corruption.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: asked the Prime Minister regarding CPIB's investigation of six former employees of Keppel Offshore & Marine Limited (KOM) for the bribery of Petroleo Brasileiro SA (Petrobas) officials (a) whether KOM’s parent company then, any officer of the parent company at the material time or any other entity or person was investigated for facilitating the bribery of Petrobas officials under the Prevention of Corruption Act 1960; (b) if so, what are the findings from the investigations; and (c) what is the conclusion from these investigations.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: asked the Prime Minister since 2000, how many (i) warnings (ii) stern warnings and (iii) prosecutions have been initiated by the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: asked the Prime Minister how will the decision not to prosecute the six individuals who were involved in the Keppel Offshore & Marine Limited corruption case in Brazil likely to affect the reputation of Singapore and Singaporean companies for having a policy of zero tolerance towards corruption.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: asked the Prime Minister (a) whether the decision not to prosecute the six individuals who are involved in the Keppel Offshore & Marine Limited corruption case in Brazil represents a departure from the Government's stated stance of zero tolerance towards corruption; and (b) whether the said decision will have an impact on deterring Singaporeans at home or abroad from committing corrupt acts in a manner that makes prosecution similarly difficult.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: My response to these Parliamentary Questions would also effectively address the Parliamentary Questions (PQs) by Members Ms Hazel Poa and Ms He Ting Ru for written answer today; and the PQs by Members Mr Dennis Tan, Mr Gerald Giam, Dr Wan Rizal1 and Ms Poa2 scheduled for subsequent Sittings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Members may wish to raise any supplementary questions arising therefrom and withdraw the PQs for later Sittings which are answered today.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Before I answer these questions, let me deal with a preliminary point.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There has been a fair bit of speculation on why the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (CPIB) did not issue a fuller statement or why the Government is dealing with the matter in Parliament, which is based on a lack of understanding of how these matters are usually dealt with.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, CPIB had explained the reasons for its decision in its press release.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With your leave, Mr Speaker, may I ask the Clerks to distribute copies of the press release to Members?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Members may also access the handout through the SGParl MP mobile app.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You would see, at paragraph 5, that CPIB explained: "This case is complex and transnational, involving multiple authorities and witnesses from several countries.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are evidentiary difficulties in cases of such nature.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Many of the documents are located in different jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition, key witnesses are located outside of Singapore and cannot be compelled to give evidence here.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The decision whether to prosecute the six individuals for criminal offences has to take into consideration all relevant factors, such as the culpability of each individual, the available evidence and what is appropriate in the circumstances.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Having taken these into consideration, stern warnings were issued to the six individuals." Police and other law enforcement agencies investigate a vast number of cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When they do not proceed, the standard practice is not to issue any statement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Where there is public interest in knowing more details, Members may file questions in this House.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the relevant Minister will, after consulting the PP who made the decision independently, answer the questions to the extent permitted in law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is what is happening here, in this case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think Members will agree, in general, when the law enforcement agencies do not proceed to charge someone after completing investigations, it is not expected that the agencies go into details of the decision.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But if anyone has questions on the decision, the matter can be raised in Parliament and that is what we are doing now.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, the reasons for issuing the stern warning rather than prosecution and the sufficiency of DPA and SOF.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Decisions on charging are made by the PP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In deciding whether to charge, the PP has to consider whether he has the necessary evidence to prove that those individuals were involved in certain conduct and possessed a certain mental state, to establish the offences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this case, as CPIB explained in its media release, there are evidentiary difficulties in doing so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To date, the findings from these requests are insufficient for prosecution, as I will elaborate later.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Given this reality, I would like to know if any Member thinks that, nevertheless, even without sufficient evidence, the PP should have proceeded to bring charges against individuals who deny the allegations against them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If so, please let me know and the basis on which you say so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Does the fact that KOM had entered into DPA make a difference in this matter?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And would the DPA be enough to, at least, commence prosecution against the specific individuals in question?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The DPA and related documents were entered into between KOM, the US Department of Justice and the US Attorney's Office.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: KOM USA, a wholly-owned subsidiary of KOM, also entered into a plea bargain agreement with the US authorities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: While the documents make reference to the actions of certain individuals, I have been advised that those references, on their own, are insufficient to establish any offences beyond reasonable doubt, without witnesses testifying in Singapore about the context surrounding those actions and the intention behind them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: CPIB conducted an in-depth investigation within Singapore, within the scope of its legal powers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, as I said earlier, the difficulty with this case is that several potentially key witnesses are not in Singapore and CPIB has not been able to secure their cooperation or agreement to testify in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With the initial assistance of the Brazilian authorities, CPIB made two fact-finding trips to Brazil in May and August 2019.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: AGC and CPIB sent three mutual legal assistance (MLA) requests to Brazil to secure the evidence that was needed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: AGC and CPIB also sent an MLA request to another relevant foreign authority to interview other potential material witnesses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is one foreign witness who gave evidence in other proceedings, which could have been relevant in establishing the offences in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, that foreign witness is not willing to voluntarily give evidence in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Neither AGC nor CPIB can compel him to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Some Members may ask whether any prosecution could be advanced arising out of the fact that a particular individual had entered into a plea bargain in another jurisdiction, in relation to his involvement in the KOM bribery.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When this individual was investigated by CPIB on his return to Singapore, he denied knowing that commissions paid to the agent in Brazil were paid out as bribes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He did not, during CPIB's investigations, implicate himself or any others in conspiring to pay bribes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Even if the PP applies to a Singapore Court to admit the plea agreement, the agreement did not identify any specific individuals and was made in the context of a plea bargain and will be given limited weight without further supporting evidence and in the face of potentially conflicting oral testimony.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If, subsequently, new and compelling facts come to light, it remains open for the PP to re-evaluate the decision in the light of the evolving legal and factual matrix.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Hazel Poa asked whether the decision to issue a stern warning was unanimous in AGC and CPIB, and if other agencies were consulted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Chua asked what offences were being considered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The decision not to charge is made by the PP in the exercise of his discretion and professional judgement, taking into account all relevant considerations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The PP does not tell us whether everyone in AGC agreed with him or if there were differing views, or which agencies he worked with apart from CPIB.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Nor is it our task to ask AGC to list all the agencies which were involved.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the end, what matters is the considered view of AGC, working with CPIB.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In response to Mr Chua, I am advised that relevant potential offences were considered by the PP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, on the naming of individuals, Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Gerald Giam asked about the identities or details of the six individuals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai and Ms Sylvia Lim asked whether other entities or persons were involved.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As a matter of policy, CPIB does not disclose the names of individuals unless they are charged in court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This policy is not unique to the CPIB; law enforcement agencies in the US, UK and New Zealand have a similar approach.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The principle underlying this policy is to avoid prejudicing that individual's right to due process and also avoid any presumption of guilt in the absence of any formal findings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If Members feel that hereafter, this practice should be changed and that law enforcement agencies should name all individuals who were investigated, even if in the end no charges are brought, then please say so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That would be a major change of policy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But please note, if Members want to change, then it cannot be only for this case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Members will recall that about two years ago, a question was in fact raised in this House, asking about the protections available for those whose reputations are affected by media coverage of ongoing trials of certain offences and how such reports are regulated.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng sought statistics on prosecutions and stern warnings, and Ms Poa asked if warnings were issued in other corruption cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Stern warnings are not unusual, being used in cases where there are evidential difficulties or little public interest to prosecute.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I have explained the reasons why no criminal proceedings have been brought in this matter.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In having regard to the rules of evidence, CPIB and AGC are observing the basic rules for a fair and just criminal justice system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What can be inferred from this is that while Singapore has zero tolerance on corruption, it also strongly adheres to the rule of law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked in what circumstances CPIB will investigate foreign bribery cases involving Singapore Citizens or companies under section 37 of the PCA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: CPIB will investigate all cases whether they happened locally or overseas, as long as the alleged offences fall under the ambit of the PCA and the information is credible and can be pursued.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: CPIB will investigate and submit its findings and recommendations to the PP, who will then decide if there is sufficient evidence to prosecute.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On Ms He Ting Ru and Ms Hazel Poa's questions regarding Singapore companies being convicted of corruption abroad, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) does not have such records and CPIB's records do not go as far back as 1965.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: More recently, in 2015, a Singapore company, Glenn Defense Marine Asia Pte Ltd (GDMA), pleaded guilty in the USA to bribery-related offences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: GDMA was not prosecuted in Singapore as key evidence against the company was not available here and GDMA had been dealt with in the USA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, Gursharan Kaur Sharon Rachael, the Singaporean employee of the US Navy, was prosecuted here as evidence of her corrupt conduct was available to CPIB and she pleaded guilty to those offences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked if we will amend the PCA to expand the powers of the CPIB to facilitate investigations outside jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: CPIB's powers under the PCA allow it to investigate offences committed by Singaporeans abroad but the investigations have to be conducted in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And regardless of what our law says, it is not possible for our agencies to exercise police powers in another country.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That would not be allowed or tolerated by any other country, just like we would never allow a foreign investigative agency to exercise police powers in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Think of it this way – do you think Singaporeans will or should accept that a regional police force can come into Singapore and interrogate Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Therefore, Members need to be realistic about what we can and cannot do.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Singapore companies who operate overseas do so in myriad environments, where all kinds of business practices prevail.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, what we can and should do is to insulate our companies and our system against corruption.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our companies must find a way to do business cleanly, wherever they do business and people must know that is how we operate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The CPIB has done its best, including working with international partners to uncover such evidence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Both are necessary factors and our zero tolerance policy must be upheld in a manner that complies with the rule of law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The PP has acknowledged this and this is exactly what the PP has done on the facts – to uphold the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I refer to the Minister's extended reply in January 2018, shortly after news of the deferred prosecution agreement came to light and the Workers' Party Members of Parliament filed a series of questions in Parliament and the Minister replied to those.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Arising out of that Sitting, I had a supplementary question about the knowledge of the Keppel Board of Directors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister replied to say that the current Board of the Directors of Keppel Corporation and its unit, KOM, "were not aware of the legal payments made to secure projects in Brazil." Can I confirm if investigations included determining the constructive knowledge of Keppel Board of Directors at the material time that corrupt payments were made to secure contracts in Brazil?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That means, not the current board that the Minister referred to in 2018, but at the material time when corrupt payments were made to secure contracts in Brazil.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second supplementary question pertains to Member of Parliament for Hougang, Mr Dennis Tan, who had filed three separate PQs seeking an update on the Keppel case in 2018, 2019 and 2022.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the final reply, the Government said that it had requested for further mutual legal assistance from foreign authorities to obtain additional information from the witnesses and the Government was still awaiting a response.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: All in all, how many mutual legal assistance (MLA) requests were made by the Government to various governments?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And was the nature of the information sought, such that it would suggest a successful prosecution would have been possible?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because from some of these earlier replies, it would appear that a witness testimony was forthcoming but that further clarifications were required.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, was it a case that there were repeated MLAs that could have helped?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Or was it a case that the Government concluded this is not going anywhere?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to the last question on whether a successful prosecution could have been mounted depending on the nature of the information, the short answer is: you do not know until you actually get the information.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not know all the details of the MLA, but I do know that the latest ones, there have been no response.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I mean, if the Member is asking what could have been done, the answer is, we do not know because they made the request and they have not been able to get the evidence that is needed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, with respect to the first question about whether CPIB had investigated the constructive knowledge at the material time of the Board, can I just seek to understand: is the Leader of the Opposition indicating or suggesting that constructive knowledge is an offence under the PCA?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My simple query was in relation to the reply that the Minister gave in 2018.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Minister directed me at that point to a Keppel press release which indicated that the current Board of Keppel was not aware of these corrupt payments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, my supplementary question today deals with the constructive knowledge of the Board at the material time, not the current Board that was referred to in 2018 – because these corrupt payments actually go back, well before 2018.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the answer that I had given previously, I had directed the Members to the Keppel press release which talked about the then current Board.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just a quick clarification on the reply from Minister on constructive knowledge.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the point, really, is not whether that in itself is an offence, but what that can lead to, in terms of identifying individuals who could be identified as knowing more and being aware of or signing off on cheques or whatever the payment process was of corrupt payments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is about the entire corpus of facts and how that could potentially identify individuals for prosecution, since Keppel was already dealt with as a corporate entity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But all in all, how many MLA requests were put?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And it would appear from the reply that the Minister had given to the Member for Hougang, Mr Dennis Tan, in 2022, I will just quote from the reply: "The Keppel Offshore & Marine case is complex and transactional in nature involving multiple foreign authorities and several more potential witnesses based overseas." Several more potential witnesses. "We have requested mutual legal assistance from foreign authorities to obtain additional information from these witnesses and are still awaiting the response to these requests." So, it appeared that there were responses to mutual legal assistance requests.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But in the latest one that was put out, there were no replies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This is what I understood from the Minister.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I think what we have from my previous answer is three to Brazil and one other, since I said, "sent an MLA request to another foreign authority".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And, as I explained earlier, they have not yielded the evidence that could be used to secure a conviction or the responses have not been helpful.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And I do understand that, at least, for one or two of them, the latest ones, there have been no response.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because you would recall earlier, when PQs were asked, or I think, in Committee of Supply (COS), I had said they were pending responses – if you recall.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There has been no further response since then.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The other question that the Leader of the Opposition asked, the thrust of his question on the Board of Directors, was whether or not there was anything in the investigations with Keppel that could lead to more evidence with respect to the individuals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This much I can say – whatever CPIB has been able to do or to uncover or to ask in its investigations in Singapore with respect to Keppel, it has done.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the problem is not so much what they had been doing the investigations here.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is the hurdle that they have not been able to overcome.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And that is why charges have not been proffered.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have Clementi residents, some who worked for Keppel in the early days of Singapore's developments, and they and their families are saddened and distressed to hear about what happened with Keppel Offshore & Marine.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Prime Minister said, and I quote, "We will never tolerate corruption.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We will not accept any slackening or lowering of standards.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Anyone who breaks the rules will be caught and punished." In conjunction with this, can I confirm with the Minister that every effort will continue to be made internationally through MLAs as needed, working with other overseas authorities, to obtain additional facts as needed that may be required to bring persons responsible to justice as far as it is possible within Singapore's laws and legal ambit?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In particular, the current AG said, and I quote, "If we are convinced that a serious offence has been committed, we will not hesitate to act, simply because securing a conviction may be an uphill task." Can I ask the Minister if we are aware of the assessment by the AG and the Public Prosecutor – the Minister said it did not reach the threshold for beyond reasonable doubt – was it assessed that the prosecution would be an uphill task in and of itself or outright impossible given the available facts?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In that speech, in the same speech, the AG actually said this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He said – he was describing the kind of internal process that the AGC goes through – and he said, "At the end of this internal Inquiry, we make an assessment of whether we are likely to have a reasonable prospect of obtaining a conviction.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Only when we are convinced that the evidence and the law disclose a criminal offence do we even begin to consider whether prosecutorial discretion should be exercised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It would be a subversion of the rule of law and a waste of valuable public resources for us to pursue prosecution in the absence of a reasonable prospect of conviction.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In fact, many of the files that were considered in my Chambers are closed at the first stage of assessment because the facts of the law do not disclose any criminal offence that can be proved in a Court of Law." And the background of that speech was that the AG was actually talking about the context of offences against minors, where it is particularly difficult to get evidence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That was the overall context he was talking about.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the question is not whether or not it was a choice between an uphill task – in other words, do not do it just because it is a bit difficult or – the other, that it is outright impossible.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The correct test is what the AG has described – it is that there must be a reasonable prospect of obtaining a conviction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, in her answer, she stressed on the fact that CPIB and AGC's assessment were that there was unavailable evidence, unavailable witnesses in jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But I think she will appreciate that under our law, confessions actually are a useful piece of evidence on which prosecutions can be mounted.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like to ask Minister, first, did CPIB interview all the six persons who were warned personally in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And secondly, in relation to this, was CPIB not able to obtain any incriminating statement from these six persons?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second clarification is, in her answer, she also referred to a foreign witness whom she mentioned could have provided useful evidence in Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And if that is so, is she saying that whatever he told the US court, in terms of the fact that he drafted agreements to facilitate the bribery scheme in conjunction with approval from his seniors, whoever they are, he is repudiating all that now in front of CPIB?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Number two: she said that some Members may ask whether prosecution could be advanced arising out of the fact that a particular individual had entered into a plea bargain in another jurisdiction – so, that is a separate individual – in relation to his involvement in the KOM bribery.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And when this individual was investigated by CPIB on his return to Singapore, he denied knowing that commissions paid to the agent in Brazil were paid out as bribes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And he did not, during CPIB's investigations here, implicate himself or others in conspiring to paid bribes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the question is, has he said something different here?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister referred to my PQ and said I asked what was the policy of CPIB, in relation to dealing with foreign bribery vis-à-vis citizens of Singapore and companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I just want to clarify that my PQ was only in relation to citizens of Singapore – and that is because section 37 of PCA excludes companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My first supplementary question is whether it may be an opportune time to review section 37 to include legal persons, such as companies, to give better bite to the rationale behind section 37 – dealing with foreign bribery?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The second supplementary question concerns the office of the Attorney-General.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Here, it is clear that the Attorney-General, in his discretion, made the decision not to proceed with prosecution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that he occupies a high constitutional office, the importance of trust between the Attorney-General's Office and the people of Singapore cannot be overstated.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For the Judiciary, they can explain their decisions through judgments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder whether structurally anything can be done to allow the Attorney-General to explain his decisions in certain cases, such that the trust between the people and the Attorney-General is always maintained.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to review of the PCA, our general assessment is that the PCA does have sufficient powers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But if there is anything that can be usefully reviewed, anything that we feel can be enhanced or improved, we are always open to suggestions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the second, on the Office of the Attorney-General, it is an office which carries a heavy responsibility.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In discharging that responsibility, the Attorney-General has to be quite careful of what he says or does not say in public, particularly with respect to decisions because you do not know whether further down along the line, a certain further action may have to be taken.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, what I have said earlier is that, in this case, they have put out as much as they thought would be appropriate to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But you really do not want a system where, every single case, the investigations are discussed in detail and where it then becomes an exercise of the public determining guilt or innocence in the absence of proper due process.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is whether or not the six executives authorised the payment of the bribes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And second, are they aware of the payment of the bribes?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And, if so, what did they do with the information?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Could Mr Louis Chua please repeat the questions?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The first is whether or not the six executives involved, authorised the payment of the bribes?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: And second, are they aware of the payment of the bribes?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: And if they are, what did they do with the information?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The short answer is, I do not know.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not know because I did not conduct the investigations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And what I do understand from the investigations is that CPIB says that the six have not made any admissions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Leader of the Opposition – just a quick one.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just a request perhaps to allow for a few more minutes to have some Members ask a few more questions on this subject, given the public interest in this issue.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If there are new questions apart from whatever has been answered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Perhaps another five to 10 minutes, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not wish it to appear that we are not responding to questions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But I hope that the Members ask questions that will be relevant and appropriate questions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I hope that if Members do have questions, do not go round and repeat the same things again.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Leader, if you could just perhaps raise a Suspension of Standing Orders to allow for the extension.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDERS (Extension of Question Time)

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And if there is sufficient evidence to pursue that and to bring it to Court, then they will do so.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If the suggestion is that we are somehow condoning bribery overseas, the answer is no.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In fact, I would direct the Member to the answer that I gave earlier on – and it bears repeating – where I said that Members need to be realistic about what we can and cannot do.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Singapore companies that operate overseas do so in myriad environments, where all kinds of business practices prevail.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, what we can do and we should do is insulate our companies and our system against corruption.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our companies must find a way to do business cleanly wherever they do business and people must know that is how we operate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are 20 countries in that category; there are 27 countries who are doing a bit better in categories 3, 2 and 1.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My question here is what are the plans of the Government to improve the effectiveness of law enforcement so that cases like these in future are less likely to slip through the cracks?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So far, in all the replies given by the Minister, I have not heard any concrete plan to improve the extent of law enforcement against acts committed abroad, not domestically.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think, domestically, we are doing well, in terms of the Transparency International reporting.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But what are we going to do differently and do better in terms of enforcing the law aboard?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My second supplementary question is, we have talked about the insufficiency of evidence to mount charges.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What then is the basis on which the stern warnings were issued?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to the first question on what can be done with respect to acts committed abroad, the first thing to remember is that the Singapore Government does not run these private companies that operate abroad.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is a matter for the companies own corporate governance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But as a Government, what we do is that we make sure our laws are directed at ensuring that you have good corporate governance; we also encourage programmes which require good corporate governance; we have a very strong stance on anti-corruption; all the signals that we send as a Government is to tell our companies, "Please – do business properly".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is incumbent upon those companies – not the Government – to ensure that their staff, their practices are clean and above board, and in accordance with proper governance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the second question, I am not sure I got that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Given the insufficiency of the evidence to mount charges, what then is the basis for the stern warnings?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But at the same time, you do not have enough to clear that evidentiary huddle.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The choices are: do nothing at all or bring charges when you know you do not have sufficient evidence; or is there something in between?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It signals; it is an expression of AGC's position that: "We do not think that you are completely off the hook, but we do not have enough to charge you; and I want you to know this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am putting down a marker, a marker that there is something not entirely right.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But this is the only device available to the AGC." So, that is what it does.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It would be a very different thing, for example, if AGC had just thrown up its hands and said, "Okay, close investigation; do not do anything." That, too, would not have been the correct thing to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I appreciate the Minister's response that it is impossible to entirely govern the way that private companies may conduct their businesses abroad.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But by the same token, perhaps, part of the concern here is that Keppel is a government-linked corporation (GLC).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I wonder if there are any general stipulations or guidelines that the Government does provide to government-linked companies about the appropriate conduct of their businesses abroad, above and beyond just saying that it is up to their own individual corporate governance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I will give the reference in a minute.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the facts of this particular case for Keppel, as part of the DPA, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim may not recall this, but Members who were present in 2018, when I responded to this in Parliament, will recall.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in this particular case, conditions were imposed; and it is my understanding that they have indeed been carried out because the DPA has been successfully concluded.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At that time, if I recall correctly, Temasek, as well as Keppel, also stated that they carry out programmes which are designed to make their staff and their companies aware of the need for good corporate governance; and that they had education programmes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think the same would be true of all other multinational corporations (MNCs).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I would agree with Assoc Prof Jamus Lim that it is very important because directors, boards, offices of companies especially large ones and especially those operating in other jurisdictions do need to be aware of the need of proper governance, anti-corruption and good controls.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: [Pursuant to Standing Order No 22(3), provided that Members had not asked for questions standing in their names to be postponed to a later Sitting day or withdrawn, written answers to questions not reached by the end of Question Time are reproduced in the Appendix.]
